paragraphs: What was called the People in the most democratic republics of antiquity was very unlike what we mean by that term. In Athens all the citizens took part in public affairs, but there were only 20,000 citizens among more than 350,000 inhabitants. All the rest were slaves, and they carried out most of the duties that belong today to the lower or even the middle classes. Athens, then, with her universal suffrage, was after all merely an aristocratic republic in which all the nobles had an equal right to govern. The struggle between the patricians and plebeians of Rome must be seen in the same light. It was simply an internal feud between the older and younger branches of the same family. All the citizens belonged, in fact, to the aristocracy and shared its character.

It should also be noted that among the ancients books were always scarce and expensive, and that very great difficulties stood in the way of publishing and circulating them. These circumstances confined literary tastes and habits to a small number of men, who formed a small literary aristocracy drawn from the choicer spirits of the great political aristocracy. Accordingly, nothing suggests that literature was ever treated as a trade among the Greeks and Romans.

These peoples were not only aristocracies but also very polished and free nations, so they naturally gave their literary productions the defects and the merits that mark the literature of aristocratic ages. Indeed, a very superficial look at the literary remains of the ancients is enough to convince us of this. Those writers were sometimes lacking in variety, or in fertility of subject, or in boldness, liveliness, or power of generalization in their thoughts, but they always showed exquisite care and skill in their details. Nothing in their works seems done hastily or at random. Every line is written for the eye of the connoisseur and is shaped by some conception of ideal beauty. No literature shows more boldly than that of the ancients the fine qualities in which the writers of democracies are naturally deficient. No literature, therefore, ought to be studied more in democratic ages. This study is better suited than any other to fight the literary defects inherent in those ages. As for their more praiseworthy literary qualities, these will spring up of their own accord, without any need to learn how to acquire them.

It is important that this point be clearly understood. A particular study may be useful to the literature of a people without being suited to its social and political needs. Suppose people persisted in teaching nothing but the literature of the dead languages in a community where everyone is habitually driven to make vehement efforts to increase or maintain his fortune. The result would be a very polished but very dangerous race of citizens. Their social and political condition would make them feel, every day, wants that their education would never teach them to supply. They would disturb the State in the name of the Greeks and Romans, instead of enriching it by their productive industry.

Clearly, in democratic communities both the interest of individuals and the safety of the commonwealth require that most people receive a scientific, commercial, and industrial education rather than a literary one. Greek and Latin should not be taught in every school. But those whose natural disposition or fortune destines them to cultivate letters, or prepares them to enjoy letters, must be able to find schools where they can gain a complete knowledge of ancient literature and where the true scholar can be formed. A few excellent universities would do more toward this goal than a vast number of poor grammar schools, where unnecessary subjects, badly learned, get in the way of sound instruction in necessary ones.

All who aspire to literary excellence in democratic nations ought often to refresh themselves at the springs of ancient literature. There is no more wholesome course for the mind. I do not hold that the literary productions of the ancients are beyond reproach. But I think they have some special merits, admirably suited to counterbalance our particular defects. They are a prop on the side where we are in most danger of falling.
